industry_name: Women at senior-IC to first-line-leader level in commercial construction, engineering, industrial manufacturing and enterprise tech (US, $110k+)

rejected_alternative.disqualification_reason: Demographic, not industry. No shared fulfilment structure, vocabulary, price ceiling or buying trigger across constituent fields. Scores 19/30 with two 2s and fails the non-industry filter outright.

demographics.job_title: Project manager, project engineer, superintendent, estimator, design engineer, engineering manager, senior/staff engineer, operations manager
demographics.location: United States, metro markets with pay-transparency legislation prioritised

problems: At least twice at site meetings, I was assumed to be the engineer's secretary sent to take minutes
There have been several incidences where I have been 'called-out' as a female and made to feel like I do not belong
People are still surprised to find a female superintendent, or women in the construction industry in general
Vastly outnumbered and have to prove themselves so much more than men
Need to prove credibility while being mindful of how they present themselves
Women who negotiate are perceived as demanding and bitchy, whereas men are seen as 'good negotiators'
negative_circumstances: Raised a solution in the meeting and was ignored; her manager later said 'What Jill said'
Told she was 'being too emotional' when she raised not getting credit for her work
A lot of people made fun of me and tried to sabotage my business, or take credit for the successes I have had
I just don't want to feel like a cog in a machine
Described as 'pushy' and 'aggressive' where men doing the same get 'go-getter' and 'leader'
Offer rescinded two days after the recruiter said she would ask for more; 'had no idea if that had anything to do with it'
My biggest hurdle was age, not gender. Being the youngest, you're always the person who knows the least
desired_outcomes: Women aren't just looking for guidance, they need champions who will advocate for them in the rooms where decisions are made
I knew my worth and showed it to them
I wanted to get into a union skilled trades job, and this was the stepping stone I needed to boost my confidence and my resume to get me there
I hope to work my way up to becoming a superintendent one day
My leadership style is a lot softer than many. In NAWIC, I can practice my leadership style. It has really helped me to grow my abilities and my confidence
I really wanted to do something in the trades
It is really rewarding. People light up when you're there. You get to be a hero
A mentor talks to you, a sponsor talks about you

icp_definition.verbatim_status: COMPLETE: 22 statements sourced (7 problems, 7 negative circumstances, 8 desired outcomes) plus a 12-point statistics layer. Fidelity caveat: quoted fragments returned by search index; source pages could not be opened from this environment (egress policy blocks direct fetching; Reddit blocks the crawler). 90-minute link-verification pass required before use in paid copy. See 01-phase1-market-icp.md section 1.7.

statistics_layer.interrupted_or_mistaken_for_junior: 7 in 10 women in construction (NCCER + Ambition Theory, n=775, 2025)
statistics_layer.want_career_growth: 87%, fewer than half have a program, 42% of those say it prepares them (same)
statistics_layer.poor_leadership_as_exit_reason: 68%, ahead of low pay and physical demands (same)
statistics_layer.onlys: 1 in 5 women; ~90% microaggression exposure vs 64% overall; 2.6x; 1.5x more likely to consider leaving (McKinsey/LeanIn)
statistics_layer.sponsorship_effect: Sponsored employees promoted at ~2x rate; 31% of entry-level women have a sponsor vs 45% of men; mentorship shows no correlation with promotion, sponsorship does
statistics_layer.engineering_pay_gap: Women engineers in the US earn ~10% less in comparable roles (IEEE Spectrum)

research_findings_that_changed_the_build: Mechanism was incomplete: 68% leave over leadership not pay, and sponsorship rather than mentorship predicts promotion. Added step 6 (the proxy ask) to the Warmth Anchor Sequence.
Buyer rejects gender-first framing in her own words ('My biggest hurdle was age, not gender'), and skews senior. Copy must open on mechanic and money, not grievance.
'Mistaken for someone more junior' is the strongest hook available: 7 in 10 prevalence, two independent verbatim confirmations, and she has a memory of it from this month.
